# Choosing Data {#sec-choosing-data}

If returns on data diminish because most examples repeat what is already learned
([Why Power Laws: The Long Tail](13-why-power-laws.qmd#sec-long-tail)), then choosing which
examples to keep, label or train on should help. A whole literature does this: deduplication,
pruning by difficulty, active learning, loss-based selection, domain mixtures and large-scale
filtering. Its reverse is training on data a model generated, which chooses badly by
construction. Every one of these methods pulls the same lever, the sampling distribution $q$,
and every one works only under a condition. This chapter measures four of the conditions and
states the rest from their sources.

## The problem

Given more candidate data than can be used (or labeled, or trained on), which examples should
the model see? When does choosing beat drawing at random, and when does it do harm?

## Assumptions

1. **Selection changes $q$, deliberately.** The chosen examples are not a sample of $p$, so
   anything estimated from them, including the model's own validation error, is biased unless
   corrected ([The Data-Generating Process](01-the-data-generating-process.qmd#sec-dgp)).
2. **Each demonstration uses the testbed that makes its condition exact:** T3 for pruning
   (example difficulty known), T4 for deduplication (duplicates and entropy rate known), T1 for
   active learning (Bayes rule known), and T2 for synthetic data (the tail known).
3. **Large-scale methods are stated, not reproduced.** Their results are labeled as reported,
   with dates.

## Derivation or demonstration

**Pruning by difficulty (replicated finding with conditions; the crossover is from one theory
paper, 2022).** Sorscher et al. analyze pruning in the teacher–student perceptron, the setting
of T3. Their result: "with abundant (scarce) data", retain only hard (easy) examples, and with
an increasing pruning fraction error can fall faster than a power law, given "a high-quality
data pruning metric" [@sorscher2022beyond, abstract].
On T3 with 100 dimensions, keeping half the examples by their true margin:

- **scarce data** ($P/N = 1$): keeping the easiest half gave test error {{< var ch14.easy_scarce >}},
  the hardest half {{< var ch14.hard_scarce >}}, a random half {{< var ch14.random_scarce >}};
  hard beat easy in {{< var ch14.hard_wins_scarce >}} of 20 seeds;
- **abundant data** ($P/N = 16$): hardest half {{< var ch14.hard_rich >}}, easiest
  {{< var ch14.easy_rich >}}, random {{< var ch14.random_rich >}}; hard beat easy in
  {{< var ch14.hard_wins_rich >}} of 20 seeds
  (`tests/test_pruning.py::test_pruning_crossover_hard_when_abundant_easy_when_scarce`).

In between, at $P/N = 4$, hard won in {{< var ch14.hard_wins_mid >}} of 20. Real difficulty
scores estimate the margin. Paul et al.'s EL2N (the norm of a model's error vector early in
training) and GraNd (the expected gradient norm) [@paul2021deep], Toneva et al.'s forgetting
events [@toneva2018empirical], and scores from small proxy models [@coleman2019selection] all
do so. Ayed and Hayou report that random pruning "outperforms most existing data pruning
methods in the high compression regime" and prove limits for score-based pruning
[@ayed2023data, abstract].

{{< include ../includes/cards/difficulty-pruning.md >}}

**Deduplication (replicated finding).** Lee et al. found near-duplicates and long repeated
substrings in standard language-model corpora: "over 1% of the unprompted output" of models
trained on them was copied verbatim, and one 61-word sentence was repeated "over 60,000 times".
Deduplicated models emitted memorized text "ten times less frequently" and reduced train–test
overlap [@lee2021deduplicating, abstract]. On T4, 50 of 400 documents were each copied five
extra times, and a trigram model that can memorize documents was trained on an 80/20 split:

- **with duplicates across the split** ({{< var ch14.dedup_overlap >}}% of test documents also
  in training): the measured test cross-entropy was {{< var ch14.opt_contam >}} nats lower than
  on fresh text, between {{< var ch14.opt_contam_min >}} and {{< var ch14.opt_contam_max >}}
  across 20 seeds;
- **deduplicated before splitting:** within {{< var ch14.opt_dedup_abs_max >}} nats of the
  fresh-text value
  (`tests/test_dedup.py::test_deduplication_reduces_overlap_optimism`).

On a long tail, deduplication also has a second role, measured in
[Why Power Laws](13-why-power-laws.qmd#sec-long-tail): it stops labels being spent on covered
cases.

{{< include ../includes/cards/deduplication.md >}}

**Active learning.** Uncertainty sampling "queries the instance whose posterior probability of
being positive is nearest 0.5" [@settles2009active, §3.1]. On T1, starting from 10 random
labels and adding 90 one at a time, it reached a rule closer to the Bayes rule than random
labeling when the classes were nearly separable: at 100 labels it had
{{< var ch14.al_ratio_clean >}} times random's disagreement (Bayes risk
{{< var ch14.bayes_clean >}}). The gain vanished as label noise grew: the ratio was
{{< var ch14.al_ratio_noisy >}} at a Bayes risk of {{< var ch14.bayes_noisy >}}, and
{{< var ch14.al_ratio_very_noisy >}} at higher noise (60 seeds;
`tests/test_active_learning.py::test_uncertainty_sampling_gains_shrink_with_label_noise`). Near
a noisy boundary, the most uncertain examples are mostly noise. A 20-seed pilot suggested that
uncertainty sampling was worse than random there; with 60 seeds the difference was within noise.

{{< include ../includes/cards/uncertainty-sampling.md >}}

**Selection by learnability (single study, 2022).** Mindermann et al. select, within each
batch, the points whose training loss most exceeds an "irreducible holdout loss": the loss of
a small model trained on holdout data. This avoids points that are already learned and points
that are noisy, which plain high-loss selection picks. They report reaching target accuracy in
18 times fewer steps on a web-scraped, noisily labeled benchmark [@mindermann2022prioritized].

{{< include ../includes/cards/rho-loss.md >}}

**Mixtures and filtering at scale (reported, 2023–2024).** DoReMi sets the proportions of
training domains with a small proxy model trained by group distributionally robust
optimization. It reports reaching a baseline's downstream accuracy "with 2.6x fewer training
steps" [@xie2023doremi, abstract]. DataComp makes dataset filtering itself the benchmark,
with a pool of 12.8 billion image–text pairs [@gadre2023datacomp]. FineWeb documents a
15-trillion-token web dataset and ablates its curation choices [@penedo2024fineweb]. Goyal et
al. show that the best filter depends on the training budget: limited high-quality data
"rapidly loses its utility when repeated", so data curation "cannot be agnostic of the total
compute" [@goyal2024scaling, abstract].

{{< include ../includes/cards/domain-mixtures.md >}}

{{< include ../includes/cards/filtering.md >}}

**Training on generated data (replicated finding, with a contested scope).** Shumailov et al.
report that training on model-generated data loses the tails of the original distribution
[@shumailov2023curse; @shumailov2024ai; an author correction was published in 2025,
@shumailov2025correction, whose content could not be accessed]. Dohmatob et al. derive the
consequence on Hutter's model. A generator fit to $t_0$ samples cuts the tail, and a learner
trained on its output plateaus [@dohmatob2024tale, Thm 2.1 and Cor. 2.2]. Gerstgrasser et al.
find that collapse follows when synthetic data *replaces* real data, and is avoided when the two
*accumulate* [@gerstgrasser2024model]. On T2 ($\alpha = 1$, $t_0 = 10{,}000$ draws per
generation, 20 seeds), the mass outside the generator's support was {{< var ch14.collapse_g0 >}}
in the first generation, equal to Hutter's expected error at $t_0$
({{< var ch14.hutter_e_t0 >}}). Replacing the data each generation, it grew to
{{< var ch14.collapse_g9 >}} by the tenth. Accumulating, it never grew
(`tests/test_collapse.py::test_refitting_on_own_samples_loses_tail`). A learner trained on
generated data can never get below that lost mass, however much it sees
(`::test_training_on_generated_data_plateaus_at_the_lost_mass`).

{{< include ../includes/cards/synthetic-data.md >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Result: every way of choosing data rests on a condition"}
Choosing data changes $q$, and each method helps only when its condition holds. Keeping hard
examples needs abundant data. Uncertainty sampling needs labels whose noise is small near the
boundary. A test set needs to be deduplicated against training. Loss-based selection needs a
way to tell unlearned from unlearnable. Training on generated data needs the real data kept,
because a generator fit to finite data has already lost the tail.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="In practice"}
Deduplicate before splitting, exactly and then approximately. Prefer weighting to discarding
when unsure. Before trusting a selection method, compare it with random selection at the same
budget, on your data, with several seeds. Keep the real data you have: if synthetic data is
added, add it, never substitute it.
:::

## What it does to the learned model

Selection changes what the model sees, so it changes what the model is good at. Pruning toward
hard examples spends the budget near the boundary; keeping easy ones teaches the bulk first.
Active learning, by design, makes the labeled set unrepresentative of $p$. Training on generated
data teaches the generator's distribution, tail missing. In every case the model's own
validation numbers, if computed on the selected data, describe $q$, not $p$.

## Failure modes

![Panel A: on T3, test error after keeping the hardest, easiest or a random half of the examples, against the examples per dimension (20 seeds). Panel B: on T4 with duplicated documents, measured minus fresh-text cross-entropy, with duplicates across the split and after deduplication (20 seeds). Panel C: on T1, uncertainty sampling's disagreement with the Bayes rule relative to random labeling at 100 labels, as label noise grows (60 seeds). Panel D: on T2, the mass outside a generator's support over generations, replacing versus accumulating data (20 seeds). Every way of choosing data rests on a condition.](../images/choosing_data.png){#fig-choosing-data}

@fig-choosing-data shows the four conditions failing:

- **Pruning the wrong end** for the amount of data (panel A).
- **Evaluating on duplicates** (panel B).
- **Querying noise** (panel C).
- **Replacing real data with generated data** (panel D).
- **Selection tuned at one scale used at another.** A filter or mixture chosen for one compute
  budget can be wrong for another [@goyal2024scaling].

## What the toy cannot show

Each testbed isolates one condition. Real selection methods face several at once, use estimated
scores instead of true margins and posteriors, and run at scales where comparing with random
selection is itself expensive. The large-scale results above are reported by their authors, on
their data, as of their publication; they are not reproduced here.
